objective: At the owner's request ('Yes, let's continue.', approving LOGIC-CIRCLE-20261107-001's recommendation): can a law with no coins have a round circle? The pinwheel tiling (Conway-Radin) is generated by one substitution of the right triangle with legs 1:2 and forced by local matching rules; its tiles turn through the irrational angle arctan(1/2). Serves question 9 (space from a law). Standalone value relative to the nearest known work: Radin and Sadun (Comm. Math. Phys. 177, 1996) proved that shortest paths along pinwheel tile edges, measured by Euclidean length, have length R + o(R), and Radin (1993) that the pinwheel system is uniquely ergodic under translations with complete rotational symmetry. Here the distance is bond distance, which counts distinctions and uses no lengths. A: an isotropy principle (a rotation-invariant hull, uniquely ergodic under translations, makes every rigid-motion-covariant bond distance round), applied to the pinwheel's parity laws; the same substitution with legs 1:1 gives a periodic triangulation whose circles are polygons with rational pi. B: exploratory measurement of the circles of the pinwheel, of the same five copies cut frame-consistently, and of the 1:1 triangle's substitution, at growing radius, and of how slowly the pinwheel's circle rounds off.
status: Complete 2026-11-07: round without coins. A law with no coins has a round circle: the parity laws on the Conway-Radin pinwheel tiling, whose bond distance (a count of distinctions, no lengths) is asymptotically the same in every direction (proved by an isotropy principle, citing Radin's unique ergodicity and rotational symmetry; Radin and Sadun had shown it for Euclidean edge length). Roundness needs both an irrational angle and mirror-image siblings: the 1:1 triangle's substitution is the periodic tetrakis triangulation (octagon pi = 10/3, square pi = 4), and the same 1:2 triangle cut frame-consistently keeps one frame and a growing four-fold component (measured). It is a large-scale trend: O(log R) orientations within radius R, anisotropy 1.106 -> 1.030 from R = 8 to 128. Next: Continue, the pinwheel grown with nothing drawn.
stop_rule: Stop when the pinwheel laws' circles are proved round or the argument is obstructed, the 1:1 law's circles are identified, and the declared measurements are recorded; do not tune a substitution toward roundness after seeing results.
title: Round without coins: the pinwheel law
